Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

simFastBOIN 2.2.0.9000

Development version. It adds designs to the single-agent BOIN design: the iBOIN design of Zhou et al. (2021), which brings prior information on the DLT probability of every dose into the decision boundaries, the gBOIN design of Mu et al. (2019), which decides from toxicity grades instead of from the DLT alone, the gBOIN-ET design of Takeda et al. (2022), which finds the optimal biological dose from graded toxicity and graded efficacy, and its time-to-event version, the TITE-gBOIN-ET design of Takeda et al. (2023). For two drugs given together, it adds the waterfall design of Zhang and Yuan (2016), which finds the MTD contour, and for the optimal biological dose the U-BOIN design of Zhou, Lee and Yuan (2019), which weighs the response against the toxicity by the utility of the joint outcome of a patient. Existing functions keep their results.

iBOIN

  • iboin_boundary() tabulates the escalation and de-escalation boundaries of the iBOIN design from a skeleton, the prior DLT probability of every dose, and a prior effective sample size, by equations 3 and 5 of the article. The boundaries depend on the dose and on the number of patients treated there, and reproduce Table 1 of the article. Where the closed form puts the escalation boundary above the de-escalation boundary, the integer boundaries with the smallest probability of an incorrect decision are searched. The robust prior of the article is available (robust = TRUE). It has a print() method.

  • iboin_simulate() simulates iBOIN trials in C++ (src/iboin_core.h). The trials run as BOIN trials with the boundaries of iboin_boundary(); dose elimination and the safety stopping rule keep the uniform prior of the BOIN design. With a prior effective sample size of 0 the trials are, for the same seed, those of boin_simulate().

  • iboin_select_mtd() selects the MTD with the prior information in the estimates of the DLT probabilities, (n_tox + prior_ess * skeleton) / (n_pts + prior_ess), or from the data alone. Only doses given to patients can be selected, and the elimination uses the data alone.

  • sim_iboin() and sim_iboin_multi() give the operating characteristics in one and in several scenarios. Their results print like those of sim_boin() and enter oc_results() and oc_compare() under the name iBOIN. The MTD is selected with the prior information by default (select_with_prior): the article gives both selections without saying which one its simulation study uses, and its operating characteristics are reproduced with the prior information and not without it.

  • inst/reproduce/reproduce_Zhou2021.R reproduces the 100 boundaries of Table 1 of the article exactly and compares the rows BOIN, iBOIN and iBOINR of Table S.1 of its supporting information (10 scenarios, 5 quantities each) with simulations: 144 of the 150 values lie within simulation error. The other six are the percentage of patients above the MTD in Scenarios 2 and 10, where the published values agree with the percentage of patients treated at doses whose true DLT probability exceeds 0.40; they are registered in inst/validation/explained.csv.

  • The C++ core was compared trial by trial with an implementation of the rules of the article in Python on the same random numbers (18 settings of 3,000 trials, no difference), and without prior information with the BOIN core.

gBOIN

  • gboin_simulate() simulates gBOIN trials in C++ (src/gboin_core.h) for a toxicity outcome with several categories that each carry a score, such as the equivalent toxicity score of Yuan et al. (2007). The scores are divided by their maximum and their total at a dose takes the place of the number of DLTs: the design escalates when the mean score is at most lambda_e and de-escalates when it is at least lambda_d, the BOIN boundaries for the target. A dose is eliminated when the posterior probability that its mean score exceeds the target, evaluated at the total score, is above the cutoff (elim_rule = "posterior", the rule of the article), or when the total score reaches the elimination boundary of the number of DLTs (elim_rule = "count", the rule of the ‘UnifiedDoseFinding’ package). One random number is drawn per patient, so that two categories of scores 0 and 1 give, for the same seed, the trials of boin_simulate(). The total normalized score of a dose is the total of the scores as given, divided once by the largest score, as in gboin_et_simulate(): with scores that are binary fractions, such as 0, 0.5, 1 and 1.5, the total is exact and the decisions are the same on every platform.

  • gboin_select_mtd() selects the MTD from the total scores by the isotonic regression of the BOIN design.

  • sim_gboin() and sim_gboin_multi() give the operating characteristics in one and in several scenarios, with the average number of patients of each toxicity category at each dose. Their results print with the labels of a score and enter oc_results() and oc_compare() under the name gBOIN.

  • The continuous end points of the article (normal distribution, total toxicity burden) are not implemented.

  • The C++ core was compared trial by trial with an implementation of the rules in Python on the same random numbers (17 settings of 3,000 trials under each elimination rule, no difference), and with two categories with the BOIN core.

  • inst/reproduce/reproduce_Mu2019.R reproduces the 14 boundaries of Table 2 of the article and compares the operating characteristics of its Table 5 (10 scenarios, the selection percentage and the number of patients of six doses) with simulations under elim_rule = "posterior": 101 of the 120 cells lie within simulation error and two hold misprints, registered in inst/validation/explained.csv. The other 17 cells, seven of them in Scenario 10, do not agree, and the reason was not found; they are left as they are.

  • inst/validation/compare-with-UnifiedDoseFinding.R compares the selection percentages and the numbers of patients of the same ten scenarios with the ‘UnifiedDoseFinding’ package: under elim_rule = "count", the rule of that package, all 130 values agree within simulation error.

gBOIN-ET

  • gboin_et_simulate() simulates gBOIN-ET trials in C++ (src/gboinet_core.h) for a toxicity outcome and an efficacy outcome with several categories that each carry a score, such as the equivalent toxicity score and the equivalent efficacy score of Takeda et al. (2022). The scores are divided by their maximum, and the mean scores of the patients at a dose take the place of the observed DLT and response rates in the rules of boin_et_simulate(), with posterior probabilities from the total scores. The toxicity event and the efficacy event of a patient are linked by a Gaussian copula and the category of a patient with an event is drawn independently, the joint distribution of boinet::gboinet(); boinet_compatible = TRUE gives the rules of that function. With two categories of scores 0 and 1 for both outcomes the trials are, for the same seed, those of boin_et_simulate().

  • The boundaries are those of boin_et_boundary() for the normalized targets, or the three values given through lambda1, lambda2 and eta1, for example those printed in an article: the mean scores are not multiples of 1 / n, so that boundaries rounded to two decimals can give other decisions.

  • gboin_et_select_obd() selects the OBD from the total scores with the rules of boin_et_select_obd(). The mean efficacy scores are the observed ones, those of the linear fractional polynomial of Takeda et al. (2022) (est_method = "fp_linear", fitted in C++), or those of the logistic fractional polynomial of ‘boinet’. min_obd_sample restricts the selection to doses with a minimum number of patients, six in the simulations of the article. The estimated efficacy scores and the utilities are compared after rounding to ten decimals, so that doses that are equal as fractions tie on every platform; the mean scores during the trial are computed exactly for scores that are binary fractions.

  • sim_gboin_et() and sim_gboin_et_multi() give the operating characteristics in one and in several scenarios, with the average number of patients of each category at each dose. Their results print with the labels of scores and enter oc_results() and oc_compare() under the name gBOIN-ET.

  • The C++ core was compared trial by trial with an implementation of the rules in Python on the same random numbers (18 settings of 3,000 trials, no difference), and with two categories with the BOIN-ET core.

  • inst/reproduce/reproduce_Takeda2022.R reproduces the 12 boundaries printed in the article and compares the gBOIN-ET rows of its Table 1 (10 scenarios, the percentage of early terminations, the selection percentage and the number of patients of six doses). The SAS program of the authors does not draw the categories from the probabilities of their Table S1 but one Bernoulli variate per category, the highest category that comes up being taken; the script simulates the probabilities that the program draws, and lists the other points in which the program differs from the article. Of the 130 cells, 119 lie within simulation error. Four are explained by rules of the program that the package does not have and are registered in inst/validation/explained.csv: a transcription of the program reproduces them. The other 7 cells, six of them numbers of patients, do not agree, also not with the transcription, and the reason was not found; they are left as they are.

  • inst/validation/compare-with-gboinet.R compares the selection percentages and the numbers of patients of six of these scenarios with boinet::gboinet(), under four selection rules: with boinet_compatible = TRUE all 156 values agree within simulation error.

TITE-gBOIN-ET

  • tite_gboin_et_simulate() simulates TITE-gBOIN-ET trials in C++ (src/tite_gboinet_core.h): the gBOIN-ET design of gboin_et_simulate() for outcomes that are observed late, in which the next cohort is enrolled while earlier patients are still assessed (Takeda et al., 2023). The patients arrive over time as in tite_boin_et_simulate(), with the same arguments for the windows, the arrivals, the event times and the share of patients that must have finished before a decision. The mean score of a dose is the total of the scores observed so far divided by the effective number of patients, a patient still under assessment counting by the fraction of the window followed so far, and the rules of gBOIN-ET are applied to these means; the admissibility of a dose uses the scores observed so far and the number of patients treated. These are the rules of boinet::tite.gboinet(); boinet_compatible = TRUE also drops the two changes of the package described in boin_et_simulate(). The boundaries can be given through lambda1, lambda2 and eta1.

  • With two categories of scores 0 and 1 for both outcomes the trials are, for the same seed, those of tite_boin_et_simulate(), and with arrivals a fixed time apart that is longer than both windows they are those of gboin_et_simulate().

  • sim_tite_gboin_et() and sim_tite_gboin_et_multi() give the operating characteristics in one and in several scenarios, with the average trial duration. The OBD is selected by gboin_et_select_obd() from the data at the last decision; the default, the highest observed mean efficacy score among the doses up to the MTD, is the selection of the article. The results print with the labels of scores and enter oc_results() and oc_compare() under the name TITE-gBOIN-ET.

  • The C++ core was compared trial by trial with an implementation of the rules in Python on the same random numbers (22 settings of 3,000 trials, no difference), with two categories with the TITE-BOIN-ET core (4 settings) and with arrivals far apart with the gBOIN-ET core (3 settings). The counts, the stopping reasons and the selected doses are the same whether or not the compiler fuses a multiplication and an addition into one operation.

  • inst/reproduce/reproduce_Takeda2023.R compares the TITE-gBOIN-ET cells of Table 1 and of Tables S2 to S6 of the article and its supporting information (10 scenarios under three settings of the efficacy window and of the accrual, 570 cells) with simulations. The R program of the authors was written again in C++ with R’s random numbers, and the transcription reproduces all 4,560 summaries that the supporting information holds for the program exactly. The program differs from the article and from boinet::tite.gboinet() in two points: where a single dose has the highest mean efficacy score among the current dose and its neighbors, it passes that dose to sample(), which then draws from all doses up to it, and it excludes doses with the effective numbers of patients. The first point moves the published tables substantially (in Scenario 1 the percentage of correct selections is 64.3 as published and about 75 without it). The package has neither. The cells that these two points move out of the simulation error are registered in inst/validation/explained.csv, and the script also compares the simulations with the transcription of the program with the two points removed (inst/reproduce/takeda2023-tables.csv). Of the 570 cells, 273 lie within simulation error of the published tables and 297 are explained by the two points; against the program without them, all 570 lie within simulation error.

  • inst/validation/compare-with-tite-gboinet.R compares the selection percentages, the numbers of patients and the trial duration of six of these scenarios with boinet::tite.gboinet(), under four selection rules. With boinet_compatible = TRUE, all 168 values agree with that function within simulation error.

Waterfall

  • waterfall_simulate() simulates trials of the waterfall design of Zhang and Yuan (2016) in C++ (src/waterfall_core.h). The design looks for the MTD contour of two drugs given together, one MTD at every dose level of drug A, by dividing the dose matrix into subtrials that are run with the single-agent BOIN design: the first subtrial goes up the lowest level of drug B and then along the highest level of drug A, and each following subtrial runs along the row below the last candidate MTD, starting one level of drug B above it. The rules are those of BOIN::get.oc.comb() with mtd.contour = TRUE in ‘BOIN’ 2.7.2, the implementation by the authors of the article, with the same order of the random numbers. Three rules of that function are not in the article and are described in the help page: a candidate in the first column below the highest level of drug A removes the rows above it and can add a subtrial on its own row, the combinations to the right of a candidate in its row are excluded from the selection, and the trial ends when a subtrial ends without a candidate.

  • When a subtrial ends without a candidate MTD, BOIN::get.oc.comb() drops its data, so that its patients are missing from the counts and a trial stopped in the first subtrial has no patients. The package keeps these data by default; boin_compatible = TRUE drops them, and then the trials are, for the same seed, those of BOIN::get.oc.comb(). That function also takes the escalation and de-escalation boundaries from the default values of p.saf and p.tox whatever values are given; the package uses the values given.

  • waterfall_select_mtd() selects the MTD of every level of drug A from the data of a trial and the combinations excluded during it, with the bivariate isotonic regression and the rules of BOIN::get.oc.comb().

  • sim_waterfall() and sim_waterfall_multi() give the operating characteristics in one and in several scenarios: the percentage of trials selecting each combination as an MTD, the percentage selecting exactly the true MTD contour, the percentages of patients treated on, above and below the contour, and the average numbers of patients and DLTs. They have print() methods. The phase I/II extension of the article is not provided.

  • BOIN::get.oc.comb(mtd.contour = TRUE) was written again in Python with R’s random numbers. With the default seed of that function and 1,000 trials, the transcription gives all 398 cells that the article and its supporting information print for the waterfall design (Tables IV, V and S1, 14 scenarios) exactly, so the article was produced with these rules. The C++ core was compared trial by trial with the transcription on the same random numbers (41 settings with and without boin_compatible, 164,000 trials, no difference). The trials and the selections are the same whether or not the compiler fuses a multiplication and an addition into one operation.

  • inst/reproduce/reproduce_Zhang2016.R compares the 398 cells of the article with sim_waterfall() under boin_compatible = TRUE, the seed 6 and 1,000 trials, and judges them by equality with the printed digits, without an allowance for simulation error (inst/reproduce/zhang2016-tables.csv holds the cells). All 398 cells are equal. The sample sizes of Table V, which the article matched between its two designs, are in all 14 scenarios the multiples of 3 closest to the average number of patients treated, those of the dropped subtrials included.

  • inst/validation/compare-waterfall-with-BOIN.R compares every cell of the output of BOIN::get.oc.comb(mtd.contour = TRUE) with sim_waterfall() in 20 settings (seven dose matrices, cohorts of 1, 2 and 3, titration, the extra safety rule and the bound on the MTD), again by equality. All 870 values are equal.

U-BOIN

  • uboin_simulate() simulates trials of the U-BOIN design of Zhou, Lee and Yuan (2019) in C++ (src/uboin_core.h), for a binary toxicity and a binary efficacy outcome observed before the next cohort and the pick-the-winner allocation of the article. Stage I runs as the BOIN design with the target tox_upper - 0.05; once a dose has n_stage1 patients, the next cohorts escalate above the highest dose tried while its DLT rate is at most the escalation boundary, and otherwise go to the admissible dose with the largest posterior mean utility. The outcomes of a patient are drawn from the Gumbel model of the article (resp_assoc) or from given probabilities (p_outcome).

  • The article does not give the priors of its toxicity and futility rules, nor whether doses not yet tried can be assigned in stage II. Before the code was written, the design was written in Python and its simulations compared with Table 3 of the article and Tables S8 and S9 of its supporting information: Beta(1, 1) priors (prior_tox, prior_resp) and the tried doses only agree with them, and are the defaults. The decision tables of the supporting information (Tables S4 to S6) are reproduced with prior_resp = c(0.05, 0.05). The results of Scenario 7 of Table 3 agree with the rates of Scenario 7 of Table S8 rather than with those printed, and Table S8 agrees with s1 = 12 rather than with the s1 = 9 of its text.

  • uboin_utility_table() tabulates the posterior mean utility and the admissibility of a dose for every outcome of its patients, the decision tables of the article. uboin_select_obd() selects the OBD from the data of completed trials. sim_uboin() and sim_uboin_multi() give the operating characteristics in one and in several scenarios, with print() methods, and their results enter oc_results() and oc_compare() under the name U-BOIN. The adaptive and equal randomization and the version for efficacy observed late (Section 2.5 of the article) are not provided.

  • The C++ core was compared trial by trial with the implementation in Python on the same random numbers (36 settings of 3,000 trials, no difference), and the trials and the selections are the same whether or not the compiler fuses a multiplication and an addition into one operation.

  • inst/reproduce/reproduce_Zhou2019.R compares the boundaries of Table 2 and Table S2, the utility tables S4 to S6, the true utilities and the 264 simulated cells of Table 3, Table S9 and Table S8 with the package (inst/reproduce/zhou2019-tables.csv and inst/reproduce/zhou2019-utility-tables.csv hold the published values). All 264 simulated cells lie within simulation error (10,000 trials; the early stopping of Scenario 3 of Table S8, 2.7 printed and 1.33 simulated, lies close to its allowance of 1.43). The 72 boundaries of Table S2, the 163 utilities of Tables S4 to S6 and the 120 true utilities are equal to the printed values, and so are 11 of the 12 boundaries of Table 2: the article prints 0.358 for lambda_d at the target 0.30, which is 0.35852. Tables S4 to S6 judge the admissibility of all 323 counts as prior_resp = c(0.05, 0.05) does; 12 of them differ under the default prior. With the rates printed for Scenario 7 of Table 3, 7 of its 11 cells lie outside simulation error, and with s1 = 9 in Table S8, 16 of its 88 cells.

Doses with the same utility in BOIN-ET, TITE-BOIN-ET and BF-BOIN-ET

  • boin_et_select_obd(), and with it sim_boin_et(), sim_tite_boin_et() and their versions for several scenarios, compare the response estimates and the utilities of the doses after rounding to ten decimals; ties go to the lowest dose, as before. Two doses can have the same utility as fractions: with the scoring utility and its default scores, 1 DLT and 7 responses in 15 patients and 4 DLTs and 9 responses in 15 patients both give 196 / 3. Version 2.2.0 compared the utilities as computed, as ‘boinet’ does, so that rounding error decided between such doses, and the selected dose could differ between platforms (for example where the compiler fuses a multiplication and an addition into one operation). In these trials the OBD can now differ from that of 2.2.0 and from that of boinet::obd.select(), also with boinet_compatible = TRUE; the simulated trials themselves are unchanged. In 96,000 simulated trials (four scenarios, the four selection rules, with and without boinet_compatible) the selection of 2.2.0 differed from a selection in exact fractions in fewer than one trial in a thousand, and in some trials between a compilation with and one without the fused operation; the present selection agrees with the exact fractions in every trial and is the same for both compilations.

  • sim_bf_boin_et() rounds its utility in the same way, for the backfill dose and for the OBD. A backfill dose that changes changes the rest of its trial, and the trials of one simulation share one stream of random numbers, so that for a given seed the results differ from those of 2.2.0 from the first such trial on; they agree within simulation error. In 40,000 trials simulated one by one, a few trials in a thousand changed, and the present core gave the same trials with and without the fused operation.

Other changes

  • The vignettes describe the new designs: iBOIN and gBOIN in vignette("simFastBOIN-introduction"), gBOIN-ET and TITE-gBOIN-ET in vignette("simFastBOIN-boin-et"), the waterfall design in vignette("simFastBOIN-combination") and U-BOIN in vignette("simFastBOIN-boin12"), each with an example, the points in which the rules differ from the article or from the reference implementation, and the results of its reproduction and comparison scripts, which the vignettes read from the result files. The README has a section for each of them.

  • A new vignette, vignette("simFastBOIN-comparison"), sets designs side by side with oc_scenarios(), oc_results() and oc_compare(): designs that select the MTD (BOIN, iBOIN, TITE-BOIN, BF-BOIN and 3+3), the two elimination rules of gBOIN and gBOIN-ET with TITE-gBOIN-ET on their mean scores, designs that select the OBD (BOIN-ET, BOIN12 and U-BOIN) and drug-combination designs (BOIN combination, Comb-BOIN12 and BOIN-ETC).

  • The pkgdown site has an article, “How the package is checked”, that summarizes the judgments of every script in inst/reproduce/ and inst/validation/, the reasons registered in inst/validation/explained.csv and the values that fail, all read from the results files of the scripts. The article is not part of the package.

  • The pkgdown site has an article, “Computation time”, with the time that every design takes on one machine, measured by inst/benchmark/benchmark.R (run_benchmark()): the designs with a reference implementation in another R package are run by both with the same settings and the same number of trials. The results are in inst/benchmark/results/benchmark.csv. The section “Speed” of the README summarizes them.

  • The pkgdown site has a cheat sheet, a single page of cards in two columns that prints on A4 in landscape, reached by “Cheat Sheet” in the navigation bar: the designs and their functions, the decision rules, the common arguments, examples for every group of designs, the comparison of designs and the conduct of a trial. pkgdown/cheatsheet_figures.R runs its code and draws its figures.

  • The print methods of sim_boin(), sim_boin_multi() and boin_simulate() take the name of the design and the labels of the rows from the result, so that the results of iBOIN and gBOIN print through them. The output for the BOIN design is unchanged.

  • The print methods of sim_boin_et(), sim_boin_et_multi() and boin_et_simulate() do the same for the results of gBOIN-ET and of TITE-gBOIN-ET. The output for the BOIN-ET design is unchanged.

simFastBOIN 2.2.0

CRAN release: 2026-11-20

This version adds designs that decide from both the DLT and the response and select the optimal biological dose (OBD): the BOIN-ET design of Takeda, Taguri and Morita (2018) with its time-to-event (TITE-BOIN-ET) and backfill (BF-BOIN-ET) versions, the utility-based BOIN12 design of Lin et al. (2020) with its time-to-event version TITE-BOIN12 (Zhou et al., 2022), and, for two drugs given together, Comb-BOIN12 and TITE-Comb-BOIN12 (Lu et al., 2025) and BOIN-ETC (Kakizume et al., 2024). It also adds the accelerated BOIN design of Kojima et al. (2024) and functions that tabulate and plot the results of different designs side by side. Existing functions only gain arguments whose defaults keep their results, so no existing result changes.

BOIN-ET

  • boin_et_boundary() finds the boundaries lambda1, lambda2 and eta1 by the grid search of boinet::gridoptim(), and reproduces the values 0.14, 0.35 and 0.48 of the article. It has a print() method.

  • boin_et_decision_table() tabulates the decision for every number of DLTs and responses, marking the counts that make a dose inadmissible, and reproduces Table 2 of the article. It has a print() method.

  • boin_et_simulate() simulates BOIN-ET trials in C++ (src/boinet_core.h). The rules follow boinet::boinet(): the admissibility of every dose is re-derived after each cohort, an inadmissible dose is skipped, and the trial stops once a dose reaches n_earlystop patients (by default the maximum sample size). Two rules differ, to keep to the article, which does not allow dose skipping during escalation: a dose excluded by its DLT data also excludes every higher dose, as in Takeda et al. (2025) and the ‘bfboinet’ package, so that an escalation cannot skip it, and an escalation from the highest dose ends the trial when that dose is excluded (stop reason "top_dose_excluded"). boinet_compatible = TRUE applies the rules of ‘boinet’ 1.6.0 exactly, in this function and in all the BOIN-ET functions below. The DLT and the response of a patient are linked by a Gaussian copula, as in ‘boinet’, or by the correlation of the binary outcomes, as in the simulations of the article (resp_cor_type). p_eli and p_eli_resp set the rates of the rules that make a dose inadmissible, so that the rules of the article can be used as well as those of ‘boinet’.

  • boin_et_select_obd() selects the OBD from completed trials with the estimators (est_method: observed rates, model-averaged unimodal isotonic regression, or fractional polynomial logistic regression with the ‘mfp’ package) and selection rules (obd_method: the highest response up to the estimated MTD, or a weighted, truncated linear or scoring utility) of boinet::obd.select(). The selection runs in C++; the model-based estimates are computed once for every distinct set of final data.

  • sim_boin_et() and sim_boin_et_multi() report the percentage of trials selecting each dose as the OBD and the average numbers of patients, DLTs and responses at each dose, for one or several scenarios, with print() methods.

  • The C++ engine and the OBD selection agree trial by trial with a separate implementation written in Python, fed with the same random numbers. The tests compare the boundaries with boinet::gridoptim() and the OBD of simulated trials with boinet::obd.select() exactly. inst/reproduce/reproduce_Takeda2018.R reproduces the boundaries, Table 2 and Table 3 of the article, and inst/validation/compare-with-boinet.R compares the operating characteristics with boinet::boinet(), which draws its random numbers differently.

  • ‘boinet’ and ‘mfp’ are suggested packages, used by the tests, the comparison and est_method = "fp_logistic".

TITE-BOIN-ET

  • tite_boin_et_simulate() simulates TITE-BOIN-ET trials (Takeda, Morita and Taguri, 2020) in C++ (src/tite_boinet_core.h), following boinet::tite.boinet(): patients arrive over time, a pending patient counts by the fraction of the DLT or response window followed, and the decision waits while fewer than half of the patients at the current dose have finished both assessments. min_completed_share changes this share; the simulations of the article did not wait (min_completed_share = 0). The times to DLT and to response come from Weibull or uniform distributions linked by a Gaussian copula. The dose rules are those of boin_et_simulate().

  • sim_tite_boin_et() and sim_tite_boin_et_multi() select the OBD with boin_et_select_obd() and report the operating characteristics and the average trial duration, with the print() methods of BOIN-ET.

BF-BOIN-ET

  • sim_bf_boin_et() and sim_bf_boin_et_multi() simulate the backfill BOIN-ET design (Takeda, Zhu and Hirakawa, 2025) in C++ (src/bf_boinet_core.h), following bfboinet::get.oc.backboinet(): the patients who arrive while a cohort is assessed are backfilled one by one to the dose with the highest utility among the doses with a promising response rate below the current dose, the dose escalation uses the DLT rate with the boundaries of BOIN, a dose with enough patients is excluded for good, and the OBD is the admissible dose up to the estimated MTD with the highest utility. They report the OBD selection, the patients treated and backfilled, the DLTs and responses, and the trial duration, with print() methods.

  • suspend sets the share of the patients at the current dose whose DLT assessment may still be running when the next cohort starts. The default, 0, waits until the DLT outcomes of the cohort are known, the BF-BOIN-ET-C design of Takeda et al. (2025), and 0.33 gives their BF-BOIN-ET-A design. backfill_extension sets how long backfilling continues after the last cohort has been enrolled, in the unit of window; the default, 100, is the value fixed in ‘bfboinet’.

  • The utility is set by the scores psi00 (no DLT and no response), psi11 (both), psi_resp_no_dlt and psi_dlt_no_resp, which ‘bfboinet’ calls ppsi10 and ppsi01. The last two names spell out the outcome because the articles index the scores in opposite orders.

BOIN12

  • boin12_decision_table() tabulates the desirability of a dose, the posterior probability that its utility exceeds the benchmark under the quasi-binomial model, and the rank-based score of Lin et al. (2020), and reproduces all 166 cells of their Table 3. It has a print() method.

  • boin12_simulate() simulates BOIN12 trials in C++ (src/boin12_core.h): the BOIN boundaries rule out an escalation from a toxic dose, the next cohort goes to the most desirable admissible dose among the current dose and its neighbors, ties to the higher dose, and the dose exploration rule escalates after 9 patients when the dose above is untried. A dose made inadmissible by its DLT data also makes every higher dose inadmissible, and the trial stops when no dose is admissible. n_earlystop (off by default) stops a trial when the current dose has that many patients and the next cohort would stay. The engine agrees trial by trial with a separate Python implementation fed with the same random numbers.

  • Three arguments of boin12_simulate(), sim_boin12() and sim_boin12_multi() select the rules of the simulations of Lin et al.

    1. where they differ from the BOIN12 software. tie_break = "random" breaks ties of desirability at random instead of choosing the higher dose ("higher", the default). no_candidate = "stop" ends the trial without an OBD, with the stopping reason "no_admissible_candidate", when no dose allowed for the next cohort is admissible, instead of going to the nearest admissible dose ("nearest", the default). explore_from = "admissible" applies the dose exploration rule only at an admissible dose instead of at any dose ("any", the default). The last two rules are inferred from the published results, which inst/reproduce/reproduce_Lin2020.R compares with the three arguments set.

  • boin12_select_obd() selects the OBD as the admissible dose up to the MTD, estimated by isotonic regression, with the highest estimated utility: the posterior mean (est_method = "posterior_mean", the default), the observed mean or the desirability.

  • sim_boin12() and sim_boin12_multi() report the OBD selection and the patients, DLTs and responses at each dose, with print() methods.

  • inst/reproduce/reproduce_Lin2020.R compares the table, the boundaries, the example of the Supplement of Lin et al. (2020) and the BOIN12 desirabilities of Table S.3 of Zhou et al. (2022), sets 10,000 simulated trials of each of the 16 scenarios beside the BOIN12 results of Figure 3 of Lin et al. and Figures S3 and S4 of their Supplement, and inst/validation/compare-with-escalation.R compares the operating characteristics with escalation::get_boin12().

TITE-BOIN12

  • tite_boin12_simulate() simulates TITE-BOIN12 trials (Zhou et al., 2022) in C++ (src/tite_boin12_core.h) with the approximated likelihood: patients arrive over time, the DLT and the response are assessed over their windows, and the decision waits while fewer than half of the patients at the current dose have finished both assessments (min_completed_share). A pending outcome is replaced by its conditional expectation given the time followed, as in Equation (11) of the article (pending_estimate = "conditional", the default), or by the estimated probability itself ("marginal"), which reproduces the desirabilities of Table S.3 of the Supplement. The admissibility of a dose uses the same approximated likelihood, so that a response that is merely late does not exclude a dose. After the last cohort, or when n_earlystop is reached, the trial waits for every outcome and the OBD is selected from the complete data. With min_completed_share = 1 and fixed arrivals the trials are exactly those of boin12_simulate(), also with the arguments tie_break, no_candidate and explore_from of BOIN12, which tite_boin12_simulate(), sim_tite_boin12() and sim_tite_boin12_multi() share.

  • sim_tite_boin12() and sim_tite_boin12_multi() report the OBD selection, the patients, DLTs and responses at each dose and the average trial duration, with the print() methods of BOIN12.

  • The engine agrees trial by trial with a separate Python implementation fed with the same random numbers. inst/reproduce/reproduce_Zhou2022.R compares the desirabilities of Table S.3 of the Supplement and the operating characteristics of BOIN12 and TITE-BOIN12 in Figure 3 of the article.

Comb-BOIN12

  • comb_boin12_simulate() simulates trials of the Comb-BOIN12 design of Lu, Zhang, Yuan and Lin (2025) for two drugs given together in C++ (src/comb_boin12_core.h), with the utility, the desirability and the admissibility of BOIN12 at every combination. The utility pE - wT * pT of the article is psi00 = 100 * wT / (1 + wT) and psi11 = 100 / (1 + wT), and its benchmark weight w_u is benchmark_weight. A combination made inadmissible by its DLT data also makes every combination with at least the same levels of both drugs inadmissible; extrasafe and offset lower the cutoff at the lowest combination, as the article does with 0.85. The arguments tie_break and no_candidate of BOIN12 apply along both drugs: "higher" keeps the tied combinations with the highest sum of the levels and draws one of them when several remain. There is no exploration rule; with one row or one column the trials are those of boin12_simulate() without it.

  • comb_boin12_select_obd() selects the OBD combination: the DLT rates are made monotone by bivariate isotonic regression, computed in C++ to a tolerance of 1e-13, the MTD combination bounds the candidates, and the admissible candidate with the highest estimated utility is selected. Distances to the target within 1e-8 and utilities within 1e-6 count as ties, so that combinations of one block of the isotonic regression, which tie exactly, are ordered by the tie rule and not by the rounding of an iterative algorithm. The response probabilities are the posterior means of the quadratic logistic model of the article with Cauchy priors (est_method = "logistic", the default), computed by adaptive importance sampling with Halton points so that no random number is used, or the observed rates. obd_bound = "rectangle" (the default) takes the candidates up to the levels of the MTD combination, as the article states; obd_bound = "contour" bounds each level of drug B by its own MTD along drug A, the rule that reproduces the published selection percentages.

  • tite_comb_boin12_simulate(), sim_tite_comb_boin12() and sim_tite_comb_boin12_multi() simulate the TITE-Comb-BOIN12 design of the same article, in which the DLT and the response may be observed late: the rules of Comb-BOIN12 at the decision times and with the interim estimates, admissibility and quasi-events of TITE-BOIN12 (src/tite_comb_boin12_core.h), and the trial durations. pending_use = "utility" counts the pending outcomes only in the utility, as Sections 2.2 and 3.1 of the article state the rules, the decision and the admissibility using the observed outcomes. With accrual = "fixed" and min_completed_share = 1 the trials are those of comb_boin12_simulate() with the same seed, and with one row of combinations those of tite_boin12_simulate() without exploration.

  • sim_comb_boin12() and sim_comb_boin12_multi() report the selection, the patients, DLTs and responses at every combination and the selection of and the patients at the true OBD combinations and at the combinations above the DLT limit, with print() methods. oc_results() and oc_compare() accept their results.

  • The engines and the selection agree trial by trial with a separate Python implementation fed with the same random numbers, and the logistic estimates agree with long Markov chain Monte Carlo runs within 0.01. When psi00 + psi11 is 100, combinations with the same numbers of patients, DLTs and responses tie exactly, whatever the rounding of the two scores; BOIN12 and TITE-BOIN12 now compute their quasi-events in the same way (no change with whole numbers psi00 and psi11, such as the defaults).

  • The documentation of comb_boin_select_mtd() now states the effect of the small amount added to the isotonic estimates correctly: among equal estimates it favors the higher combination below the target and the lower one above it, as BOIN::select.mtd.comb() does. The selection itself is unchanged.

BOIN-ETC

  • boin_etc_simulate() simulates trials of the BOIN-ETC design of Kakizume, Takeda, Taguri and Morita (2024) for two drugs given together in C++ (src/boin_etc_core.h): the dose matrix is divided into subtrials along which the DLT probability increases, and BOIN-ET (with the boundaries of boin_et_boundary()) is run in each of them until the next combination has n_earlystop patients. subtrials = "etc1", "etc2" or "etc3" are BOIN-ETC1, 2 and 3 of the figures, tables and code of the article (its Section 2.2 describes BOIN-ETC2 and BOIN-ETC3 the other way round). A combination excluded by its DLT data also excludes the higher combinations of its subtrial, the subtrial ends when its lowest combination is excluded, and the trial ends when that combination is A1B1. etc1_start chooses the starting combination of a row of BOIN-ETC1, one level of drug B below the previous candidate ("diagonal", the text and figures of the article, the default) or at the same level ("below", the code of the authors), and rule4 = "authors_code" applies the choice among the neighboring combinations of the code of the authors, which moves one combination down when the combination below the current one is untreated. Only etc1_start = "below" with rule4 = "authors_code" reproduces the published allocation of BOIN-ETC1.

  • boin_etc_select_obd() selects the optimal dose combination: the DLT rates are made monotone by unweighted bivariate isotonic regression, computed in C++ to a tolerance of 1e-13, the MTD combination of every row (the highest of the tied ones, within 1e-8) bounds the candidates of that row, and the treated, not excluded candidate with the highest posterior mean of the utility is selected. odc_tie = "all" counts every tied candidate, the definition of the percentages of the article.

  • sim_boin_etc() and sim_boin_etc_multi() report the selection, the patients, DLTs and responses at every combination and the selection of and the patients at the true optimal combinations and at the combinations above the target, with print() methods. oc_results() and oc_compare() accept their results.

  • The engine and the selection agree trial by trial with a separate Python implementation fed with the same random numbers. inst/reproduce/reproduce_Kakizume2024.R compares the allocation and the selection with Table 3 and Supplementary Tables S1 to S9 of the article, and inst/validation/compare-with-BOINETC.R runs the code of the authors in R. With the random numbers of R after set.seed(1234), the code gives the published allocation and selection of 48 of the 60 settings to the printed digits, but for values that appear to be misprints. On the same trials, boin_etc_select_obd() selects other combinations only when combinations tie for the MTD combination of a row in the exact isotonic regression, of which the code keeps those that the convergence errors of Iso::biviso() leave closest to the target, or when the code selects an untreated or excluded combination.

Accelerated BOIN

  • boin_simulate(), sim_boin() and sim_boin_multi() gain the argument titration_doses, which ends the titration at a given dose: when no DLT is seen up to it, full cohorts start at the next dose. With n_earlystop = 6 this is the accelerated BOIN design of Kojima et al. (2024), and the warning on a small n_earlystop is then not given. The default, NULL, keeps the titration of the BOIN package, and the results of earlier versions do not change. inst/reproduce/reproduce_Kojima2024.R compares Tables 1 and 2 of the article.

Tables and figures

  • oc_scenarios() tabulates scenarios of DLT and response probabilities, for a single agent or a drug combination, with the true utility of every dose and the true MTDs and OBDs. The utility takes the correlation of the DLT and the response as the simulation functions do; the true OBDs can also be given directly when an article defines them otherwise.

  • oc_results() collects the results of any of the simulation functions, of their _multi versions and of oc_3p3() into one long data frame, and oc_compare() judges them against the true doses of oc_scenarios(): selection of the true MTD or OBD, patients treated there, selection of and patients at overdoses, trials without a selection, sample size and duration. All three have print() and plot() methods.

Checks of the time-to-event and backfill designs

  • inst/reproduce/reproduce_Takeda2020.R sets the simulations beside Table 2 of Takeda et al. (2020) (TITE-BOIN-ET and BOIN-ET), and inst/reproduce/reproduce_Takeda2025.R beside Tables 1 and 2 of Takeda et al. (2025) (BF-BOIN-ET with and without the suspension rule).

  • The C++ engines of TITE-BOIN-ET and BF-BOIN-ET agree trial by trial with separate implementations written in Python from the R code of ‘boinet’ and ‘bfboinet’, fed with the same random numbers. inst/validation/compare-with-boinet.R now also compares sim_tite_boin_et() with boinet::tite.boinet(), and inst/validation/compare-with-bfboinet.R compares sim_bf_boin_et() with bfboinet::get.oc.backboinet().

Documentation

  • The new vignette vignette("simFastBOIN-boin-et") describes BOIN-ET, TITE-BOIN-ET, BF-BOIN-ET and BOIN-ETC, the selection of the OBD and the dose moves that differ from ‘boinet’, and summarizes the reproductions and comparisons from the tables of judgments that the scripts write.

  • The new vignette vignette("simFastBOIN-boin12") describes BOIN12, TITE-BOIN12, Comb-BOIN12 and TITE-Comb-BOIN12: the desirability score table, the rules of the simulations of the articles that the defaults do not follow, a comparison of BOIN, BOIN-ET and BOIN12 on the same scenarios with oc_compare(), and the reproductions and comparisons.

  • vignette("simFastBOIN-introduction") describes the accelerated BOIN design and the functions oc_scenarios(), oc_results() and oc_compare(), and vignette("simFastBOIN-combination") points to the designs that select an optimal dose combination.

simFastBOIN 2.1.0

CRAN release: 2026-10-16

This version adds the time-to-event BOIN (TITE-BOIN) design, the BF-BOIN and BE-BOIN designs, which backfill patients to lower doses while the dose escalation waits, the BOIN design for trials of two drugs given together, and a decision table for the 3+3 design. No existing function or result changes.

TITE-BOIN decision table

  • tite_boin_decision_table() tabulates the decision rule of the TITE-BOIN design, which lets new patients be treated while the DLT assessment of earlier patients is still pending. Two methods are offered: the single mean imputation of Yuan et al. (2018), method = "imputation", with boundaries on the standardized total follow-up time (STFT), and the effective sample size of Lin and Yuan (2020), method = "ess", with boundaries on the effective sample size (ESS). The table has print() and plot() methods, and the printed layout follows the published tables.

  • The suspension rules of the two articles are available for both methods: max_pending_ratio (accrual is suspended when more than half of the patients are pending, the default of the imputation method) and min_completed (escalation requires two patients with a completed assessment, the default of the effective sample size method).

  • min_follow_up adds rule 2 of Chen et al. (2025): while patients are pending, escalation requires every pending patient at the current dose to have been followed for at least this fraction of the assessment window, and accrual is suspended until then. It is available in tite_boin_decision_table(), tite_boin_simulate(), sim_tite_boin() and sim_tite_boin_multi(), and defaults to 0, which changes nothing. With max_pending_ratio = 0.49 (their rule 1 with A = 51) and min_follow_up = 0.25, the imputation method reproduces every entry of Table 1 (target 0.3) of Chen et al. (2025) and of Table A1 (target 0.25) of the supplementary materials of Chen et al. (2026), 131 states in all. The printed table shows the condition, for example >= 0.22 & MF >= 0.25.

  • With the defaults, the imputation method reproduces every entry of Table 1 (target 0.2) of Yuan et al. (2018) and Table S1 (target 0.3) of its supplementary appendix, 640 states in all, and the printed table has the same rows. The published tables allow de-escalation when the observed DLT rate equals the target, which equation (5) of the appendix, read literally, does not; the implementation follows the tables. The dose decisions of the trial example in Figure 1 of that article are reproduced as well.

  • Elimination counts the pending patients as treated without DLT, as both articles define it. States without pending patients agree with boin_decision_table().

TITE-BOIN simulation engine

  • tite_boin_simulate() simulates TITE-BOIN trials in which patients arrive over time and DLTs can occur late in the assessment window. It returns the patient and DLT counts of boin_simulate() together with the duration of each trial, the number of suspensions of accrual and the time spent suspended. The engine is written in C++ (src/tite_core.h), like the BOIN engine.

  • The dose for a cohort is decided when its first patient arrives, with the rules of tite_boin_decision_table(); the engine and the table are checked against each other at every state. A suspension lasts until the next pending patient at the current dose completes the assessment or, with a positive min_follow_up, until the minimum follow-up is reached, whichever comes first. Because DLTs can be observed after a dose has been left, the elimination rule is checked at every dose, not only the current one.

  • Times between arrivals can be exponential, uniform or fixed, and the time to DLT Weibull, with the share of DLTs in the second half of the window set by late_fraction, or uniform.

  • prior_weights weights the follow-up of the pending patients by a piecewise uniform prior for the time to DLT over the three thirds of the window, as in Appendix D of Yuan et al. (2018) and Section S1 of Lin and Yuan (2020). The decision table is unchanged; only the follow-up compared with it is. Equal weights, the default, use the unweighted computation, so the default results do not change. The weighted trials agree exactly with the separate Python implementation, which uses the formula of Lin and Yuan’s reference code.

  • One uniform variate per patient, drawn from R’s stream in the order used by boin_simulate(), decides both whether a DLT occurs and when; arrivals come from a separate generator. Whenever no patient is pending at a decision the trials are therefore identical to those of boin_simulate() with the same seed, which the tests check for both methods and several designs.

  • The trials agree exactly with a separate implementation written in Python, run on a replica of R’s random number stream.

TITE-BOIN operating characteristics

  • sim_tite_boin() and sim_tite_boin_multi() summarize simulated TITE-BOIN trials in the same way as sim_boin() and sim_boin_multi(), with the same options for selecting the MTD (bound_mtd, mtd_max_estimate, min_mtd_sample) and the same overdose component. They add the average and standard deviation of the trial duration, the percentage of trials with accrual suspended, and the average number and total time of suspensions.

  • The results inherit from the BOIN classes (c("tite_boin_oc", "boin_oc") and c("tite_boin_oc_multi", "boin_oc_multi")), so code that reads the result of sim_boin() also reads them. They have their own print() methods, which also show the design and the timing; the table of sim_tite_boin_multi() has two rows more per scenario, for the duration and the suspensions.

  • Whenever no patient is pending at a decision, every summary agrees exactly with that of sim_boin() under the same seed, including the options of MTD selection and the safety rules; the tests check this for both methods.

Backfilling: BF-BOIN and BE-BOIN

  • bf_boin_simulate() simulates the BOIN design with backfilling (BF-BOIN) of Zhao et al. (2024). The dose escalation proceeds in fully staggered cohorts with the BOIN decision table, and a patient who arrives while it waits is backfilled to a lower dose that has not been eliminated, has fewer than n_cap patients and has a response observed at or below it. Doses are closed for backfilling, and conflicts between the backfilled doses and the current dose are resolved with pooled data, as in Table 2 of the article.

  • be_boin_simulate() simulates BE-BOIN of Chen et al. (2026), which combines backfilling with TITE-BOIN. The escalation decides while patients are pending, with rules 1 and 2 of the article (max_pending_ratio = 0.49 and min_follow_up = 0.25), and every estimate imputes the pending patients, over several doses with equation (2) of the article.

  • sim_bf_boin(), sim_be_boin(), sim_bf_boin_multi() and sim_be_boin_multi() summarize the simulated trials. The results inherit from the BOIN classes, count backfilled patients among the patients treated, and add the backfilled patients and the responses at each dose, the trial duration, the waits of the escalation and the patients turned away. The MTD is selected from the data of all patients, as in sim_boin(). They have their own print() methods, and the table of the _multi functions has seven rows per scenario.

  • Points that the articles leave open are arguments: no_slot decides whether a patient with nowhere to go waits or is turned away, conflict_dose whether the highest (Zhao et al., 2024) or the lowest (Chen et al., 2026) conflicting dose anchors the pooled estimate, and backfill_dose which open dose receives a backfill patient. The time to response is Weibull (resp_window, resp_late_fraction), and the DLT and the response are linked by a Gaussian copula (resp_cor, 0 by default), as in Takeda et al. (2025).

  • The engine is written in C++ (src/backfill_core.h). The DLT variates of the escalation are drawn from R’s stream as in boin_simulate(); arrivals, backfill patients and responses have generators of their own. When no dose is ever opened for backfilling the trials are identical to those of boin_simulate() (BF-BOIN) and of tite_boin_simulate() (BE-BOIN with no_slot = "wait") with the same seed, which the tests check.

  • With stay_on_1_of_3 = TRUE, n_earlystop = 9, accrual = "uniform" and no_slot = "leave", the operating characteristics of Table 4 of Zhao et al. (2024), twelve scenarios of BF-BOIN and five of BOIN, are reproduced within simulation error, durations included; over 20 seeds of 10,000 trials the largest gaps were 2.1 points for the selection, 0.4 patients and 0.17 months. The article states a Poisson process of arrivals, but its durations agree with uniform times between arrivals and patients turned away while the escalation waits. inst/validation/compare-with-Zhao2024.R repeats the comparison.

  • The trial examples of Figure 1 of Zhao et al. (2024) and of Section S2 of the supplementary materials of Chen et al. (2026) are replayed patient by patient, and the simulated trials agree exactly with a separate implementation written in Python, over 2,700 trials of both designs.

BOIN design for drug combinations

  • comb_boin_simulate() simulates the BOIN drug-combination design of Lin and Yin (2017), which looks for a single MTD in a matrix of dose combinations of two drugs. After each cohort the decision of the single-agent design is taken at the current combination; an escalation goes one level up of either drug, and a de-escalation one level down, to the neighbor with the larger posterior probability that its DLT rate lies between the boundaries. The engine is written in C++ (src/comb_core.h) and follows BOIN::get.oc.comb() with mtd.contour = FALSE: the same rules, applied in the same order, with the random variates drawn in the same order, so that with the same seed the two produce the same trials.

  • comb_boin_select_mtd() selects the MTD combination from completed trials, with the bivariate isotonic regression of Iso::biviso(), the routine the reference implementation calls. Combinations that the regression pools are equal in exact arithmetic but can differ in their last digits, and these digits decide between combinations on the same anti-diagonal, so another algorithm would select differently in a few trials out of a thousand. The ‘Iso’ package, which version 1.4.0 moved to Suggests, is therefore imported again.

  • sim_comb_boin() and sim_comb_boin_multi() summarize the simulated trials: the selection percentage and the average numbers of patients and DLTs at every combination, the percentages of trials selecting a true MTD combination and of patients treated at one, and the exposure to combinations above overdose_cutoff. They have their own print() methods, and the table of sim_comb_boin_multi() has one row per scenario.

  • comb_boin_next() gives the combination for the next cohort of a trial in progress, from the numbers of patients and DLTs observed at every combination and the combination of the last cohort. It reports the boundaries that apply, the two candidates with their posterior probabilities and scores, both candidates when they tie, the combinations eliminated, and why the trial stops when it does. It has print() and plot() methods; the plot draws the dose matrix with the data, the current and next combinations and the eliminated ones. The decision is taken by the same C++ code as in the simulations (comb_decide() in src/comb_core.h), so a trial is run with the rules whose operating characteristics sim_comb_boin() reports. These differ from BOIN::next.comb() in three respects: BOIN::next.comb() stops as soon as n.earlystop patients have been treated at the current combination, blocks an escalation of one drug when a combination at the next level of that drug has an observed DLT rate at or above lambda_d, and breaks ties at random. The tests check that comb_boin_next() takes the decision of simulated trials after every cohort, and that it agrees with BOIN::next.comb() on random data wherever the rules coincide. The C++ code also takes the same decision as the Python implementation at each of the 40,664 states reached by 3,300 simulated trials in 11 settings.

  • The tests reproduce the example of Yan et al. (2020): every number printed by summary() in the article agrees to the printed precision. The one average exactly half-way between two printed values, 1.905 patients at A2B4, is printed 1.90 in the article and 1.91 by R 4.6.0; how such a value is rounded depends on the version of R. The tests also check exact agreement with BOIN::get.oc.comb() in nine settings whenever the BOIN package is installed. The simulated trials also agree exactly with a separate implementation written in Python and run on a replica of R’s random number stream, over 5,500 trials in 11 settings. inst/validation/compare-comb-with-BOIN.R extends the comparison with BOIN to 200 configurations, and inst/validation/compare-with-LinYin2017.R sets the results beside Tables 2 and 3 of Lin and Yin (2017), whose rules differ in some details.

  • The waterfall design of Zhang and Yuan (2016), which looks for the MTD contour, and a time-to-event version of the drug-combination design are not provided.

3+3 decision table

  • decision_table_3p3() tabulates the rule of the 3+3 design used by oc_3p3() and sim_3p3(): the decision at three and at six patients during dose escalation and, for mtd_rule = "expand", during the search for the MTD that follows. It has print() and plot() methods in the style of the BOIN decision table. The tests follow the table through every possible course of a trial and obtain the operating characteristics of oc_3p3().

Documentation

  • A second vignette, vignette("simFastBOIN-tite"), describes the TITE-BOIN design. The introductory vignette gains a pointer to it and a paragraph on decision_table_3p3(). The README describes the design, how it is checked, and its speed: 10,000 trials of five doses and 20 cohorts of three take 0.09 s with the imputation method and 0.11 s with the effective sample size, against 0.05 s for sim_boin() on the same machine.

  • The labels of plot.tite_boin_decision_table() are shorter, the codes over the boundaries (for example E/S over >=2.15), so that they fit in the cells.

  • A third vignette, vignette("simFastBOIN-backfill"), describes the BF-BOIN and BE-BOIN designs, and the README and the introductory vignette point to it.

  • The DESCRIPTION cites the two TITE-BOIN articles and the three articles on backfilling and its suspension rules.

  • A fourth vignette, vignette("simFastBOIN-combination"), describes the drug-combination design, and the README and the introductory vignette point to it. The DESCRIPTION cites Lin and Yin (2017). The vignette also shows the decision table for a protocol and how to run a trial with comb_boin_next().

  • A pkgdown configuration (_pkgdown.yml) groups the reference pages by design and lists the four vignettes as articles.

  • The plot() methods of boin_decision_table(), tite_boin_decision_table() and comb_boin_next() draw the legend key of every decision or status, including those that do not occur in the figure, which ggplot2 3.5.0 and later otherwise leave blank.

simFastBOIN 2.0.0

CRAN release: 2026-09-18

The first release since 1.3.2, and a breaking one. Versions 1.4.0 and 1.5.0 were development versions on GitHub and were never released; their entries are kept below because the changes they describe are all part of this release. Anyone upgrading from 1.3.2 should read the 1.4.0 entry, which lists the renamed functions and the corrected defects.

This section covers three design options requested for a quality control review. Every new option is off by default, so a simulation run with version 1.4.0 arguments produces exactly the same trials, selections and summary figures. Two names in the returned objects did change, and are listed under their respective headings below: overdose60 and overdose80 moved into the new overdose component, and one reason code was renamed.

Staying on one DLT out of three

  • stay_on_1_of_3 makes one DLT out of three patients a stay rather than a de-escalation, which is the modification offered by the BOIN web application. It is available on boin_boundary(), boin_decision_table(), boin_simulate(), sim_boin() and sim_boin_multi().

    The option raises the de-escalation boundary at three patients from one DLT to two, so exactly one cell of the decision table changes and nothing else moves. It is applied only where one DLT out of three currently de-escalates: it never overrides an escalation, and it never overrides an elimination, which is a safety rule. boin_boundary() reports whether it took effect in stay_on_1_of_3_applied.

    With the default thresholds it takes effect for target rates from about 0.098 to 0.279. Note that the web application describes the range as 0.25 to 0.279; the upper end agrees, but the lower end is 0.098, below which one DLT out of three already eliminates the dose.

Bounding the MTD by a stated DLT rate

  • mtd_max_estimate caps the isotonic estimate a dose may have and still be selected as the MTD, on boin_select_mtd(), sim_boin() and sim_boin_multi(). It changes only the selection, never the dose-finding, so the decision table is untouched.

    bound_mtd caps the estimate at the de-escalation boundary, which always lies above the target rate. A cap at or below the target therefore cannot be expressed with bound_mtd at all, and needs mtd_max_estimate.

  • The reason code "no_dose_below_lambda_d" returned by boin_select_mtd() is now "no_dose_below_bound", since the bound need not be the de-escalation boundary.

Exposure to overly toxic doses

  • sim_boin() and sim_boin_multi() gain overdose_cutoff, and report an overdose component describing how far patients were exposed to doses whose true DLT probability exceeds it:

    • pct_patients, the percentage of all simulated patients treated at such a dose, that is the probability that a patient is dosed above the cutoff;
    • pct_patients_by_trial, the same percentage computed within each trial and then averaged;
    • avg_n_patients, pct_trials_any, pct_trials_over_60 and pct_trials_over_80.

    and how often the design ends up recommending such a dose, which is a separate question from exposure during the trial:

    • pct_trials_mtd_above, the percentage of all trials whose selected MTD is above the cutoff;
    • pct_mtd_above_when_selected, the same among the trials that selected an MTD at all.

    The cutoff defaults to target, which reproduces the earlier behavior.

  • This replaces the overdose60 and overdose80 components of the result, which are now overdose$pct_trials_over_60 and overdose$pct_trials_over_80. They are reported as zero rather than NA when no dose exceeds the cutoff, and the doses component names the dose levels that do.

Choosing a de-escalation boundary directly

  • boin_p_tox() returns the value of p_tox for which the de-escalation boundary equals a stated value, inverting boin_lambda(). A design team that wants to tighten the boundary usually states the boundary rather than the threshold behind it, and this turns that statement into the argument the other functions take.

    A boundary close to the target needs a threshold close to the target, and the rest of the package refuses a p_tox within ten percent of target. The inverted value is still returned, but a warning names the smallest boundary that leaves a usable threshold: about 0.315 for a target of 0.30.

Printing

  • print() on the result of sim_boin_multi() gains percent and digits, which the method for a single scenario already had. Passing percent = TRUE to the cross-scenario method previously fell into ... and was ignored, so the counts were printed as though nothing had been asked for.

Documentation

  • start_dose, added in version 1.4.0, is now documented as being ignored when titration = TRUE, because the titration phase always begins at the lowest dose. This matches the reference implementation.

  • The spelling throughout the documentation is now the United States spelling declared by the Language field, and tests/spelling.R keeps it that way. The colours argument of plot.boin_decision_table() is renamed colors accordingly. The argument was introduced in version 1.4.0, which was never released, so no released code is affected.

The 3+3 design as a comparator

  • oc_3p3() returns the operating characteristics of the traditional 3+3 design. The probability of every path the design can take is evaluated in closed form, so the result carries no Monte Carlo error and takes no seed. sim_3p3() simulates the same design and is there to confirm the closed form. Both return an object of class oc_3p3 whose components carry the same names as those of sim_boin(), so the two designs can be tabulated side by side, and print() lays them out the same way.

  • mtd_rule selects between the two definitions of the MTD in common use. "previous" names the dose below the one declared too toxic. "expand" takes the MTD to be the highest dose at which at most one of six patients had a DLT, expanding a dose that has only three patients before assessing it. Neither is universally the standard, so the comparator being matched should be checked before a rule is chosen. The two agree on which doses are visited during escalation, and therefore on the probability that a patient is exposed to an overly toxic dose; they differ in the sample size and in the selection percentages.

  • overdose_cutoff works as it does for sim_boin() and defaults to one third here, which is the rate the regulatory question is asked about. The 3+3 design has no fixed maximum sample size, so the within-trial exposure percentage and the 60 percent and 80 percent thresholds reported for BOIN have no counterpart and are not returned.

Validation

  • inst/validation/compare-with-BOIN.R compares the package against BOIN over 200 configurations, five dose-toxicity scenarios by five designs by eight option combinations, and covers extrasafe, titration and boundMTD. All 200 agree to within floating point on the selection percentages, the patients and DLTs at each dose, the percentage of trials ending without an MTD and the totals. This is a defect test rather than a Monte Carlo comparison, because the two implementations draw the same variates in the same order for a given seed. The options that BOIN has no counterpart for are checked separately, to confirm that each leaves the simulated trials untouched when it is off.

simFastBOIN 1.4.0

This is a substantial revision. The simulation engine has been rewritten in C++, the user-facing functions have been renamed, and several defects that affected numerical results have been corrected. Results obtained with version 1.3.2 are not reproduced by this version, even with the same seed.

Exact agreement with the BOIN package

The engine now draws one uniform variate per patient, in enrollment order, and applies the decision rules in the same order as BOIN::get.oc(). With the same seed and matching arguments the two implementations agree trial by trial rather than only on average. The test suite checks this directly against BOIN::get.oc() and BOIN::get.boundary() when the BOIN package is installed.

Version 1.3.2 claimed in its README that random number generation was the same as that of the BOIN package when the seed was fixed. That claim was incorrect, because trials were generated across trials rather than one at a time, and it has been removed.

Corrected defects

  • max_total_pts was computed as n_cohort * cohort_size[1], so a trial with a vector cohort_size used the wrong maximum sample size. It is now the sum of the cohort sizes.

  • With titration = TRUE and a vector cohort_size, the titration phase tested if (cohort_size > 1) on a vector, which stops with an error on R 4.2 and later.

  • The early stopping rule at n_earlystop was evaluated after the dose had already been changed, and therefore against the wrong dose. It is now evaluated at the dose that was just treated, before the transition, as in the reference implementation. This changes operating characteristics, in particular when a de-escalation lands on a dose that has already accrued n_earlystop patients.

  • MTD selection now re-derives dose elimination from the final data of the trial instead of carrying the elimination status over from the dose-finding stage. The two differ when a trial ends at its maximum sample size, because the last cohort was then never checked against the elimination boundary.

  • The isotonic fit used for MTD selection is now computed over the admissible doses only. Previously every treated dose entered the fit, so an eliminated dose could change the estimates at the doses below it and hence the selected MTD.

  • The tie-breaking perturbation was applied twice, once inside isotonic_regression() and once inside select_mtd(), and was indexed by dose level rather than by position in the admissible set. It is now applied once, during MTD selection, and boin_isotonic() returns the unperturbed estimates.

  • get_pts_and_tox() called set.seed() without restoring the state of the random number generator. The new functions restore it on exit.

  • Random number generation was not consistent within a trial: the titration phase, the ordinary cohorts and the final partial cohort used three different schemes, the last of which drew a binomial variate. All patients now use a single scheme.

Renamed functions

The old names remain available and issue a deprecation warning, but they return the value of the replacement function, which is not the value returned by version 1.3.2. See ?"simFastBOIN-deprecated".

Version 1.3.2 Version 1.4.0
get_boin_boundary() boin_lambda(), and boin_boundary() for the integer boundaries
get_boin_decision() boin_decision_table()
get_boin_stopping_boundaries() boin_boundary(extrasafe = TRUE)
get_pts_and_tox() boin_simulate()
isotonic_regression() boin_isotonic()
select_mtd() boin_select_mtd()

sim_boin() and sim_boin_multi() keep their names.

Changed interfaces

  • The design arguments come first: sim_boin(target, p_true, n_cohort, cohort_size, ...), with n_trials now an optional argument. Calls that relied on positional matching must be updated.

  • boundMTD is now bound_mtd, and return_details is now keep_trials.

  • sim_boin() returns an object of class boin_oc directly, rather than a list with a summary element. Selection percentages, average patient counts and average DLT counts are separate components, and the percentage of trials selecting no MTD is no longer appended to the selection vector.

  • sim_boin() and sim_boin_multi() now return their result visibly, so calling them at the prompt prints the summary and assigning the result is silent. Previously the result was invisible unless verbose = TRUE.

  • sim_boin_multi() uses the same seed for every scenario. Version 1.3.2 used seed + i for the i-th scenario, so a scenario simulated in a multi-scenario run did not match the same scenario simulated on its own.

  • sim_boin_multi() accepts a plain named list of p_true vectors in addition to the list of list(name, p_true) used previously.

  • boin_select_mtd() takes the patient and DLT counts, not precomputed isotonic estimates, since the fit depends on which doses are admissible.

  • Progress messages are emitted with message() rather than cat(), so they can be suppressed with suppressMessages().

New

  • start_dose, matching the reference implementation, which did not exist in version 1.3.2.
  • boin_boundary() returns the escalation, de-escalation, elimination and safety stopping boundaries as integer DLT counts indexed by sample size, with a print method that can restrict the table to the end of each cohort.
  • boin_decision_table() returns a classed object with print and plot methods. The print method blanks the impossible combinations and can restrict the table to the sample sizes reached at the end of a cohort; the plot method draws the table as a grid of colored cells, each carrying its decision letter so that the figure does not rely on color alone. It needs ggplot2, which is suggested rather than required.
  • boin_stopping_table() lays the safety stopping boundary out as a two-row table, one column per sample size.
  • boin_simulate() returns the raw trial data with a stop_reason for every trial, and has a print method.
  • Operating characteristics now include the risk of overdosing 60 and 80 percent of patients, and the distribution of the reason for stopping.
  • Arguments are validated. Out-of-range probabilities, thresholds too close to the target, non-monotone p_true and inconsistent counts are reported instead of propagating silently.

Dependencies

  • Added Rcpp, and utils for one call to globalVariables().
  • Added ggplot2 to Suggests, used only by plot.boin_decision_table().
  • Removed Iso. The pool adjacent violators algorithm is implemented in C++; Iso is now only suggested, and used in a test that checks the two agree.
  • knitr and kableExtra moved out of Imports. knitr is suggested and used for the vignette and for the optional table output; kableExtra is no longer used.
  • utils was imported in NAMESPACE but absent from DESCRIPTION. Neither imports it now.

Performance

The C++ engine replaces the vectorised R implementation, and MTD selection no longer calls out to R once per trial. For five doses, 20 cohorts of three, n_earlystop = 18 and 10000 simulated trials, one measurement gave 9.98 seconds elapsed for BOIN::get.oc() against 0.07 seconds for sim_boin(). The ratio depends on the design and on the machine, and the README carries the code that reproduces the measurement.

simFastBOIN 1.3.2

CRAN release: 2025-12-17

New Features

Customizable Safety and Toxicity Thresholds

  • Added p_saf and p_tox parameters to core functions

    • sim_boin(), sim_boin_multi(), and get_pts_and_tox() now accept custom safety and toxicity thresholds
    • p_saf: Highest toxicity probability deemed acceptable for safety (default: 0.6 * target)
    • p_tox: Lowest toxicity probability deemed unacceptable for toxicity (default: 1.4 * target)
    • These parameters are passed to get_boin_boundary() for boundary calculation
    • Stored in summary objects for reference and reproducibility

  • Usage examples

    # Using default thresholds (0.6 * target and 1.4 * target)
result_default <- sim_boin(
  n_trials = 10000,
  target = 0.30,
  p_true = c(0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.55, 0.70),
  n_cohort = 10,
  cohort_size = 3,
  seed = 123
)

# Using custom thresholds
result_custom <- sim_boin(
  n_trials = 10000,
  target = 0.30,
  p_true = c(0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.55, 0.70),
  n_cohort = 10,
  cohort_size = 3,
  p_saf = 0.15,  # Custom safety threshold
  p_tox = 0.45,  # Custom toxicity threshold
  seed = 123
)

Documentation Improvements

  • Enhanced parameter documentation
    • Added comprehensive roxygen2 documentation for p_saf and p_tox parameters
    • All @param entries now use consistent multi-line format for better readability
    • Updated examples to demonstrate custom threshold usage
  • Expanded test coverage
    • Added tests for p_saf and p_tox parameter handling in sim_boin()
    • Added tests for p_saf and p_tox parameter handling in sim_boin_multi()
    • Added tests for p_saf and p_tox parameter handling in get_pts_and_tox()
    • Verified that custom values are correctly stored in summary objects
    • Verified that default values are correctly calculated when not specified

Breaking Changes

None. All existing code continues to work as before. The new p_saf and p_tox parameters have sensible defaults (0.6 * target and 1.4 * target respectively) that match the standard BOIN methodology, ensuring full backward compatibility.

Internal Changes

  • Updated function signatures to include p_saf and p_tox parameters with NULL defaults
  • Modified internal logic to calculate default values when parameters are not specified
  • Updated summary objects to store p_saf and p_tox values for reproducibility

simFastBOIN 1.3.1

Bug Fixes

  • Fixed DESCRIPTION Date field
    • Corrected Date from 2024-12-06 to 2025-12-06
    • This was a typo in the year field that was caught during CRAN submission process

No functional changes. All code and features remain identical to version 1.3.0.

simFastBOIN 1.3.0

New Features

Progress Message Control

  • Added verbose parameter to sim_boin() and sim_boin_multi()

    • Control whether progress messages are printed to console
    • verbose = FALSE (default): Run silently without progress messages
    • verbose = TRUE: Display progress messages as in previous versions
    • Particularly useful for R Markdown documents and vignettes where clean output is desired
    • Results are identical regardless of verbose setting

  • Usage examples

    # Silent mode (default) - ideal for vignettes and reports
result <- sim_boin(
  n_trials = 10000,
  target = 0.30,
  p_true = c(0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.55, 0.70),
  n_cohort = 10,
  cohort_size = 3,
  seed = 123
)

# With progress messages
result <- sim_boin(
  n_trials = 10000,
  target = 0.30,
  p_true = c(0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.55, 0.70),
  n_cohort = 10,
  cohort_size = 3,
  verbose = TRUE,
  seed = 123
)

Documentation Improvements

  • Standardized roxygen2 documentation format
    • All parameter descriptions now use consistent multi-line format
    • Improved readability and maintenance
    • Enhanced consistency across all functions
  • Updated vignettes
    • Clean output without progress messages
    • Better integration with R Markdown workflows
    • Improved presentation quality

Breaking Changes

None. All existing code continues to work as before. The new verbose parameter defaults to FALSE, which changes the default behavior to silent mode, but all functionality remains identical.

Migration Guide

For users who prefer the previous behavior with progress messages:

# Add verbose = TRUE to see progress messages
result <- sim_boin(
  n_trials = 10000,
  target = 0.30,
  p_true = p_true,
  n_cohort = 48,
  cohort_size = 3,
  verbose = TRUE,  # Add this line
  seed = 123
)

simFastBOIN 1.2.1

New Features: Multi-Scenario Simulation and HTML Output

New Multi-Scenario Simulation Function

  • Added sim_boin_multi() function

    • Run BOIN simulations across multiple dose-toxicity scenarios simultaneously
    • Automatically orchestrates simulations for each scenario using sim_boin()
